title: Cold White Fingers and Tight Skin / Screen the Lungs and Heart, Spare the Steroids

blocks.text: Cold White Fingers and Tight Skin / Screen the Lungs and Heart, Spare the Steroids

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-52 · Consultation · PACES Station 5 (less acute), consultation encounter · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) · 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min · Guidelines: British Society for Rheumatology, The 2024 guideline for management of systemic sclerosis, Rheumatology 2024;63(11):2956-2975 (published online 11 September 2024) · Related AMaC: Cardiovascular examination: tricuspid regurgitation with pulmonary hypertension (link when that station is published)

Dear Doctor, a 43-year-old piano teacher. Years of cold white then blue fingers, now tight skin on her hands and face, breathlessness on stairs and aching joints. Her GP has started a short course of prednisolone. Please assess and advise.
Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Raynaud's with tight skin is systemic sclerosis: screen the lungs at baseline and the pulmonary circulation every year, and minimise glucocorticoid, which raises the risk of scleroderma renal crisis (BSR 2024).

The Examiner Trap. She asks for something for her aching joints and her GP has started prednisolone. Candidates continue it. Pass: stop to review the steroid, check blood pressure and kidney function, arrange lung and heart screening. Fail: continue or raise the steroid without recognising the renal-crisis risk.

rows: Raynaud's alone or systemic disease? Get the story.
"Tell me about the fingers, the skin and your breathing. Any swallowing trouble or heartburn?"
Introduce, consent, ask about pain; Raynaud's, ulcers, skin, dyspnoea, reflux, drugs, steroid.
Look for sclerosis and organ involvement.
"May I examine your hands, face, chest and heart, and check your blood pressure?"
Hands, mouth opening, skin, telangiectasia, ulcers, lungs, JVP, P2, BP.
Screen the lungs and heart; protect the kidneys.
"This looks like scleroderma. I'd like to check your lungs and heart every year and review the steroid."
Lung tests, CT, echo, NT-proBNP; blood pressure and kidney function; steroid review.
Share the plan; find her worry.
Explain tests, treatment, alternatives; safety net; check understanding.

Offers a chaperone, warms the room and asks about her playing

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are. A 43-year-old piano teacher. Thoughtful, worried about your hands. Married with a teenage son.
Opening line. "My hands are stiff and sore and the prednisolone helps. Can I stay on it?"
Volunteered. Fingers turn white and blue in the cold for years; skin on the hands and face tightening for a year; aching joints.

Only if asked. Breathless on stairs for six months, dry cough. Heartburn most nights. Occasional trouble swallowing dry food. Tender sores at the fingertips last winter. Prednisolone 20 mg daily for a week from your GP (scenario). No headaches. No blood pressure readings at home. Non-smoker. Alcohol: a glass of wine at weekends. No allergies. No recent travel abroad. Other medicines: antacid tablets for the heartburn, nothing else. Mother has an underactive thyroid; no other family illness. Works from home teaching piano; no driving problems.
Hidden concern. You fear that you will lose the use of your hands and your teaching. Reveal only if asked what worries you most.
Your questions. "Is it scleroderma?" "Will I lose my fingers?" "Can I stay on the steroid?" "Will it affect my lungs?"
How you react. Good handling: you agree to stop and have tests. Poor handling: if the steroid is simply continued you say you feel better and take it.

Findings (released as each step is done). Sclerodactyly with tight shiny skin to the knuckles, digital pitting scars and calcinosis; tight facial skin with reduced mouth opening; telangiectasia on the face and palms. No digital ulcers today. Fine basal crackles. JVP not raised; loud P2. No oedema. BP 148/92, pulse 82 (scenario values). Lung function: gas transfer low; chest film shows basal shadowing (scenario).

Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis (R5): systemic sclerosis, limited or diffuse. Q2 Lung screening (R6): baseline high-resolution CT and lung function including gas transfer (BSR 2024). Q3 Pulmonary hypertension (R6): annual screening with lung function, echocardiography and NT-proBNP, using the DETECT tool where appropriate (BSR 2024). Q4 Kidney (R6): glucocorticoid should be minimised, with caution above 10 mg prednisolone equivalent; scleroderma renal crisis presents with new hypertension and kidney injury; check BP, kidney function and urine; ACE inhibitor started if it occurs (BSR 2024). The guideline gives no numeric blood pressure trigger: 148/92 on prednisolone is a prompt for a kidney and urine check, not a diagnosis. Q5 Advice (R7): warmth, stop smoking, reflux treatment, return with headache or high pressure.
Curveball 1. "She has headaches and a BP of 190/110." (R6) Safe: suspect renal crisis; same-day assessment, ACE inhibitor, specialist advice.
Curveball 2. "She has an infected fingertip ulcer." (R6) Safe: treat infection, specialist review.
Curveball 3. "She asks for warfarin for pulmonary hypertension." (R6) Safe: anticoagulation with warfarin is not recommended in SSc-associated PAH (BSR 2024); specialist PH centre.
Curveball 4. "I'll stay on prednisolone." (R7) Safe: capacity present; explain the renal risk, offer another way to ease the joint pain, and revisit; do not simply agree.

Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Show me your hands. [R1 Fail] (No lung or steroid history. [R2 Fail] [R3 Fail])
(Reports digital ulcers and oedema that are not there. [R4 Fail])
CANDIDATE: It's Raynaud's. [R5 Fail] Stay on prednisolone and I'll raise it. [R6 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Come back in a year. [R7 Fail]

Examiner note: No history, signs invented, wrong diagnosis. Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): continuing or raising steroid in systemic sclerosis risks scleroderma renal crisis. The examiner sees a red flag: a high-risk drug continued with no blood pressure or kidney check.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: Hello. May I examine your hands, chest and blood pressure? Tell me if anything hurts. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Tell me about the fingers, your breathing, heartburn and swallowing. Which tablets are you on? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: I'm short of breath and on prednisolone. I'm afraid of losing my hands.
CANDIDATE: That's a real worry. What concerns you most? [R3 Pass]
(Checks hands, face, mouth opening, chest, JVP and BP; finds sclerodactyly, pitting scars, crackles, BP 148/92. [R4 Pass])
CANDIDATE: This looks like systemic sclerosis. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: I'd review the prednisolone today and agree with the rheumatology team how to minimise it, because steroids can bring on a kidney crisis in scleroderma. I'd check your blood pressure now, with blood and urine tests for your kidneys, then arrange a CT and lung function, and an echo and NT-proBNP every year. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: The tests will show if your lungs or heart are involved. I recommend them. If you get a severe headache or your blood pressure is high, come in the same day. Do you understand? [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and clear, and the renal risk is named. Did not arrange home blood pressure monitoring or offer an alternative for the joint pain.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? I'll keep the room warm. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any headaches, home blood pressure readings or family history? How is your playing? [R2 High]
PATIENT: I'm afraid of losing my hands and my teaching.
CANDIDATE: Thank you for telling me. Early treatment protects function, and we'll plan around your work. [R3 High]
(Also finds calcinosis and loud P2; no oedema, no ulcers today. [R4 High])
CANDIDATE: Systemic sclerosis, limited or diffuse; overlap syndromes and drug causes are alternatives. [R5 High]

CANDIDATE: Steroids risk scleroderma renal crisis, so I'd minimise or stop it with the rheumatology team and teach you to check your blood pressure at home, with urgent review if it is high or you get a headache; an ACE inhibitor would start if the pressure rises; CT and lung function now, then echo, NT-proBNP and lung function annually; referral to a specialist pulmonary hypertension centre if needed. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: Options: screening now, or waiting, which risks missing lung or heart disease. Keep warm, stop smoking, treat reflux, and return with headache or high pressure. [R7 High]
Examiner note: Answered the fear for her hands and covered the renal risk.

R6: Continuing or raising steroid is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): it risks a scleroderma renal crisis, and a blood pressure of 148/92 on 20 mg prednisolone needs a kidney check.
R2: Not asking about breathlessness and steroid use misses lung disease and the drug risk.
R4: Reporting ulcers and oedema that are not present shows signs were assumed.
R5: Primary Raynaud's ignores tight skin and pitting.
R7: Instructions without options leave her without a say.
"Are you taking prednisolone?"
"I'd check your blood pressure and your lungs."
"What worries you most?"

BSR 2024 (published online 11 September 2024): all people with systemic sclerosis have baseline high-resolution CT and lung function including gas transfer; annual screening for pulmonary arterial hypertension (lung function, echocardiography, NT-proBNP, DETECT tool); glucocorticoid treatment minimised in adults (recommendation grade 1A; the text advises caution above 10 mg prednisolone equivalent, which is not itself a graded recommendation); ACE inhibitor started in renal crisis; self-monitoring of blood pressure in early-stage disease for high-risk people (narrative text, not a graded recommendation). Risk markers include prior high-dose steroids, hypertension and proteinuria. The guideline gives no numeric blood pressure trigger; 148/92 here is a scenario value that justifies a blood pressure trend, kidney function and urine check, not a diagnosis of renal crisis.
Warfarin is not recommended in systemic sclerosis-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension (BSR 2024); PAH therapy is started by a designated centre.
THINK: Systemic sclerosis; lungs, heart, kidneys.
SAY: "This looks like scleroderma; I'd check lungs and heart and review the steroid."
DO: Hands; face; chest; BP; CT; lung function; echo; NT-proBNP.
NUMBERS: BP 148/92 (scenario); prednisolone caution above 10 mg; PAH screening yearly (BSR 2024).
TRAP: Continuing prednisolone.
FINISH: Review the steroid; home BP and kidney check; return with headache or high BP; warmth; reflux treatment.

The 2024 British Society for Rheumatology guideline for management of systemic sclerosis. Rheumatology 2024;63(11):2956-2975 (published online 11 September 2024). https://doi.org/10.1093/rheumatology/keae394 Supports: baseline HRCT and lung function; annual PAH screening; minimising glucocorticoid; ACE inhibitor in renal crisis; no warfarin in SSc-PAH.
